To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the perceptual experience associated with viewing visual ambiguous stimuli can be stabilized and biased by the context in which the stimulus is embedded.

the perceptual interpretation of ambiguous visual stimuli can vary depending on the context in which the stimuli are presented, and that this variation can be used as a probe for the neuronal mechanisms of perceptual inference.

contextual influences on the perception of ambiguous visual displays are mediated by a number of mechanisms including temporal context through prior stimulation, temporal context through internal brain states brought by feedback from higher processing levels and spatial context.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain integrates sensory information to construct a stable perceptual experience in the presence of conflicting sensory input.
the role of context for the construction of perceptual experiences and the mechanisms that underlie this process.
how the brain resolves perceptual ambiguities and the role of contextual information in perceptual inference.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
context-driven perception of visual ambiguity is a highly complex process, involving a multitude of different mechanisms that are still not fully understood.
context is important for the brain to construct perceptually stable interpretations of ambiguous visual stimuli.
the brain's perception of ambiguous visual information is context-driven and that the brain's perceptual decision-making process is highly sensitive to contextual influences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
context-driven inference is a fundamental principle of perceptual decision making.

the perceptual stability associated with the dominant percept of an ambiguous visual stimulus is a result of the brain's ability to integrate information from multiple sources, including sensory, prior knowledge, and internal states.
context-driven perceptual decisions with ambiguous visual stimuli provide an ideal paradigm to study how the brain integrates information from different sources to make perceptual decisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain is a predictive machine that continuously integrates bottom-up sensory information with top-down contextual influences in order to make the most likely perceptual inferences about the world.
context is a critical component of perception and that the perceptual system is not a passive receiver of information, but an active interpreter and constructor of perceptual experience.
the perceptual stability of ambiguous stimuli is a function of context-driven perceptual inference.
